title: There is no largest prime
statement: For every natural number n there is a prime p with n < p. Equivalently, there are infinitely many primes.

formal.statement: theorem Nat.exists_prime_gt : ((n : AxNat) -> Exists.{1} AxNat (fun (p : AxNat) => And (AxNat.lt n p) (And (AxNat.le (AxNat.succ (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) p) ((d : AxNat) -> ((hd : AxNat.dvd d p) -> Or (Eq.{1} AxNat d (AxNat.succ AxNat.zero)) (Eq.{1} AxNat d p))))))

notes: `open` here means NOT ESTABLISHED IN THIS LEDGER; it is not mathematically open, Euclid settled it. It is recorded because it is a live target rather than a curiosity: the prelude already carries `Nat.not_dvd_one_add_mul_of_two_le`, which is exactly the step `no a >= 2 divides 1 + a*t` -- the contradiction at the end of Euclid's argument. What is missing is a least-divisor construction, and `Nat.lt_well_founded` is present to support one. formal.statement is written in the SAME core rendering the kernel emits for its own theorems, and uses ONLY symbols `build_nat_prelude` actually declares (checked against the 119-theorem inventory dumped on 2026-08-14), so it can be dispatched without inventing vocabulary. Primality is spelled out inline because the prelude has no `Prime` predicate. Binders carry readable names rather than the kernel's `x0, x1, ...`; that is a pretty-printing difference only, and any admitted proof would render with positional names.
